doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: Many influences, taking gigs, and Jason Mraz's lesson in simple ideas
summary: He balances opportunities, turned down a big country act, and learned from pop, especially Jason Mraz, to nurture simple ideas.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And when you put things on your website about what it is you do, you try to make it clear that you’re a man with many influences?
I mean if you list, when you listed some of the people you’ve played with, to me it means that you’re open to other things.
As well as the practical idea of taking a gig.
I played with Blood, Sweat & Tears. I may have loved that music and maybe I didn’t but —

There is a balancing act that goes on as a professional musician, depending on your opportunities and your interests. There are some opportunities I’ve had which I’ve had to let go because I just couldn’t sign off. You know I don’t see a place for me in country music. And I had an opportunity to play with a really big, really big country act, and I couldn’t do it. I just — I just thought okay this is crossing the line. And they are great, but you know, so you just make these decisions on a day-to-day basis. But I learned a lot about music and a lot about jazz from pop music, the good kind. And it occurred to me at a certain point that taking a simple idea and giving it lots of love and care, you know, rather than just trying to play as much as you can and play hard. You ever hear that expression? Play hard, play hard. There’s a validity to that but, you know, I’ve noticed like of my old boss, Jason Mraz, he’s a songwriter. He’s a guitar player. Not in the sense of Wes Montgomery, but in the sense of a songwriter accompanying himself. But just that attention to simple ideas. It means a lot. It means a lot when it comes to getting your point across to an audience. You know. So in improvisation I try to remember that. You know I try to be myself, I try to not be a Bill Watrous, which I could never be. I try to not be — it’s just do — my idea is that you take something simple and you nurture it. And if it then grows all these leaves so to speak then that’s fine. But at least the start of it is solid and pure and concise.
